original_value: Aiming at the problem that the weak faults of rolling bearing are difficult to recognize accurately, an approach on the basis of swarm decomposition (SWD), morphology envelope dispersion entropy (MEDE), and random forest (RF) is proposed to realize effective detection and intelligent recognition of weak faults in rolling bearings. The proposed approach is based on the idea of signal denoising, feature extraction and pattern classification. Firstly, the raw signal is divided into a group of oscillatory components through SWD algorithm. The first component has the richest fault information and perceived as the principal oscillatory component (POC). Secondly, the MEDE value of the POC is calculated and used to describe the characteristics of signal. Ultimately, the obtained MEDE values of various states are trained and recognized by being input as the feature vectors into the RF classifier to achieve the automatic identification of rolling bearing fault under different operation states. The dataset of Case Western Reserve University is conducted, the proposed approach achieves recognition accuracy rate of 100%. In summary, the proposed approach is efficient and robust, which can be used as a supplement to the rolling bearing fault diagnosis methods.

result.paraphrase: To address the difficulty of accurately recognizing weak faults in rolling bearings, a method combining swarm decomposition (SWD), morphology envelope dispersion entropy (MEDE), and random forest (RF) is proposed for effective detection and intelligent identification of weak bearing faults. The method follows the concepts of signal denoising, feature extraction, and pattern classification. First, the raw signal is decomposed into several oscillatory components by the SWD algorithm, and the first component, which contains the most fault information, is treated as the principal oscillatory component (POC). Next, the MEDE value of the POC is computed to characterize the signal. Finally, MEDE values from different states are used as feature vectors and fed into the RF classifier for training and recognition, enabling automatic fault identification of rolling bearings under varying operating conditions. Experiments on the Case Western Reserve University dataset show a recognition accuracy of 100%. In conclusion, the proposed approach is efficient and robust, and can serve as a supplement to rolling bearing fault diagnosis methods.
